desc: VASCO compares the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey plates, exposed between 1949 and 1957, against modern digital sky surveys, hunting for point sources present in the historical plates and absent today. Its methodological power is a matter of dates: the POSS-I plates predate the first artificial satellite, so a genuine star-like transient on them cannot be a satellite glint, which removes the single largest confound in any modern optical-transient search. The project published its methodology in The Astronomical Journal in December 2019; reported nine simultaneously occurring transients on a single plate from 12 April 1950 in Scientific Reports in June 2021; and argued in Acta Astronautica in May 2022 ('A glint in the eye') that photographic plate archives constitute a viable search space for non-terrestrial artefacts. On 20 October 2025 Stephen Bruehl and Beatriz Villarroel published in Scientific Reports the finding that POSS-I transients may be associated with above-ground nuclear testing and with contemporaneous reports of unidentified anomalous phenomena. That result is the most important peer-reviewed development of 2025 for this board's historical premise: it produces, in a Nature-portfolio journal and from a physical archive outside any government's classification authority, a statistical association between the American atomic-weapons complex and anomalous optical transients over the United States in the exact years the legacy programme is alleged to have begun. The Sol Foundation made it Policy Briefing No. 1 in January 2026.
